## Moving Window Approach: Condition Monitoring and Robust Power Forecasting for a Solar Farm

Kumar Saurav IBM Research Labs kr.saurav.010@in.ibm.com

Jagabondhu Hazra IBM Research Labs jahazra1@in.ibm.com

_**Abstract**_ **—Costs of PV installations has been progressively declining over the past decade and has attained grid parity in several countries. In developing countries such as India with high energy shortages and growing energy demand, new energy firms are setting up large solar farms to offering greener energy at a competitive tariffs. The fact that solar PV power is irradiance dependent make it an intermittent source of energy and thus prone to penalties while feeding the power into the national grid. Moreover, there are factors such as accumulation of dust, breakage, aging, etc. which can lead to under-performance of the solar farms, thus further reducing the profit margins. This calls for methodologies that can not only predict the power generation capacity of the solar farm accurately but also detect the underperformance, malfunction and aging of the solar panels.**

**In this paper, we propose a moving window based machine learning approach to accurately predict the energy production from a solar farm. The proposed methodology may also be used monitor the performance yields of solar farms, identification of operational problems and degradations in solar panels due to aging. We demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed approach on a 1.2MW solar farm located in a tropical country consisting of** 6 **different PV technologies of 200KW each.**

## I. INTRODUCTION

Energy share contributed by renewable sources is gradually expanding in the energy market around the world. Consumers are now more educated and care about their carbon foot print on the environment. Energy cost procured from renewable sources such as solar and wind has been progressively declining over the past decade. This declining prices of renewables, increased cost of fossil fuel coupled with the strong encouragement from the government in the form of investments and subsidies has resulted in aggressive growth in the overall deployment of these new energy sources. Countries all over the world have ambitious target to procure greater share of their energy from non-polluting, clean, and green sources. For instance, United States share of renewable energy will be 20% by 2020 and 30% by 2025 [1]. Similarly, Germany has set up a long term target of procuring 60% of total energy and 80% of electrical energy from renewable sources by 2050 [2]. Furthermore, even developing countries such as India has the target to generate 175 GW from renewable sources by 2022 which is approximately four times as compared to 46GW in 2016 [3], while China aims at getting 20% of its energy from renewables.

Power generated from solar PV is expected to have its fair share in this green energy revolution which because of no moving parts and virtually zero maintenance costs has created its niche in the energy market. A recent solar farm contract in

India, winning bid was about 2.71 INR per kilowatt hour of energy which is less than 0.05 USD/kWh [4]. However, this simplicity of solar comes along with its own sets of challenges. Power generation from solar is roughly proportional to the solar irradiance, thus making it an intermittent source of energy. Moreover, utility scale solar farms are an elaborate systems consisting of thousands of PV arrays, possibly of different technologies [5]. For such a large scale system, several factors can potentially reduce overall yield resulting in loss of revenue. Some well the known factor include physical damage to panels and inverter, accumulation of dust over the panels, browning of cells due to degradation and aging and, shading due to vegetation and other physical structures just to name a few. This motivates the compulsion for an accurate and continuous monitoring of the solar farm performance to identify under-performance and malfunctions, and to execute the subsequent course of actions accordingly [6], [7], [8].

Additionally, setting up a new solar farms calls for a significant capital investments, For example, _Kamuthi solar project_ in Tamil-Nadu state of India is a 650 MW plant whose construction cost was about 4,550 crore INR (710 million USD) [9]. Growing competition and drive to further lower the energy cost has resulted in some interesting solutions such as using ultra-low cost reflectors to create larger ground coverage at reduced number of expensive solar panels [10]. While, others have proposed using battery to store energy during the noon and feed power into the grid during periods of higher tariffs [11]. In some cases, investors purchase the farms after their operational date so as to minimize risks during construction phases. Hence, detailed monitoring is imperative to safeguard the financial investments. Further, accurate production forecast is necessary to exploit the difference in feed-in tariffs and also to avoid the penalties associated with unit commitment.

Energy output from a solar farm depends on several parameters including incident solar insolation, other weather factors (temperature) and the quality of the solar panels itself. There may be several reason other than aforementioned factors that can lead to lesser than expected power productions such as soiling or accumulation of dust [12], surrounding vegetation growth, shadowing [13], inverter malfunctions etc. This multidimensional dependence make the performance monitoring as well as accurate power forecast a challenging task. Manufacturers do provide the nameplate capacity, however those datasheets are indicative of performance only under standard condition, which rarely occur during actual field operations.

In this paper, we propose a single methodology to address

the dual problem of condition monitoring and accurate power forecasting of solar PV panels. In particular, the key contributions of this paper are:

- We propose a moving window based machine learning approach to accurately predict the power output from a solar farm. We implement the proposed approach on the data of six different PV panel technology obtained from a 1 _._ 2 MW solar farm. This farm is a cluster of six smaller farms with installed capacity of approximately 200 kW for each panel technology.

- On the same data set, we exhibit the efficacy of the proposed methodology for condition monitoring applications such as fault detection and progressive deterioration due to aging of solar panels.

- We further demonstrate the robustness of our approach in power forecasting even for under-performing panels due to malfunction and aging.

Rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section II provides a brief overview about existing research work in the literature. Section III provides the description of the solar farm and some brief analytics on the data collected. The proposed methodology is presented in section IV. Finally, concluding remarks and future works are provided in section V.

## II. RELATED WORK

Solar PV power forecasting and farm condition monitoring is a well-studied topic in the literature. For instance, a machine learning based approach is presented in [14], and a neural network based approach is used for short term forecasting in [15]. Further, researchers have used support vector machine for solar forecasting in [16] while in [17] have proposed a hybrid methodology combining several machine learning techniques such as self-organizing maps, learning vector quantization network, support vector regression and fuzzy logic to achieve a lower prediction error than the individual methods. Similarly, [18] provides forecasting for smart grid management.

On the other hand, there are several research papers on condition monitoring application in solar farms including analytical approaches and data driven methodologies. For example, [19] resents a comprehensive analysis of a 100 kWp solar power plant and [20] provides a long term performance degradation analysis for PV systems. Several publications provide a spectrum of approaches for fault detection such as comparison between expected and actual production [21], statistical analysis [22], artificial neural networks [23], etc. Another approach uses the I-V curve of the PV system and the voltage measurements to accurately estimate the farm power output [8]. However, this method can only be used for condition monitoring and not for power forecasting because, voltage measurements are not available beforehand.

Most of the aforementioned research works decouple the power forecasting with performance monitoring and hence focus only on either of the aspect. However, we believe that both are two faces of the similar problem and hence can easily be tackled using a single methodology. Therefore, in

this paper we seek to address this gap by providing a single approach which can be extended to address both the problems simultaneously. We implement the proposed approach on the data collected from a 1 _._ 2 MW solar farm located in Brunei.

## III. SOLAR FARM IN BRUNEI

In this paper, we are using a high-frequency detailed dataset obtained from a 1 _._ 2 MW solar farm for a duration of 3 years. Details about this farm is described next.

## _A. Farm Geography and Climate_

The solar farm is located in Brunei (4 _._ 5 _[o] N,_ 114 _._ 5 _[o] E_ ), a small coastal country in southeast Asia. It is situated near equator, hence has a tropical humid climate with two prominent seasons: Dry season and Rainy season. Brunei, being situated near the equator, is gifted with abundant solar energy and received bright sunshine over 300 days every year.

_C. Preliminary Data Analysis and Data Visualization_

First of all, we do a preliminary analysis of the data set to get initial insight about the nature and behavior of the solar farm. We can observe the variations in the power production across different days. Figure 1 shows the power generation profile from one set of panels for three different types of day: Mostly sunny, partially cloudy and, overcast day. Further, this will enable us to study the relationship between various features, for example, how the power generation from the solar farm is dependent on weather parameters such irradiance, temperature, humidity, wind speed, etc. and therefore, we can select the most important set of features for further analysis. In figure 2, we show the correlation between power generated by each panel technology and different weather parameters. We can observe that in all cases, power generation is highly correlated with the irradiance. Further, it is interesting to note that there is some dependence between power and temperature. However, this correlation exist mostly due to dependence of temperature on irradiance, since higher irradiance will imply a higher ambient temperature. Therefore, we can say that irradiance is the most important feature for power production.

portional. There is some minor nonlinearity and to capture that, we have used a piece-wise linear approach. Benefit of using piece-wise linear models is that, it is able to capture the nonlinear behavior yet we do not lose the simplicity of a linear model. ## IV. MOVING WINDOW BASED APPROACH

In this section we describe the proposed moving window approach where only recent past data is used for training the model. The model thus trained is used to predict the power output for the next day. In this paper, we are using past 15 days of data for training, however, this can be tweaked to suit different requirements. For example, if we want to predict solar power output on 27th June, we will use data from 11th to 26th June (15 days) and similarly, from 12th to 27th June for prediction on 28th June. This ‘Moving-Window” approach evolve over time and whatever variations happen due to soiling, dusting etc. gets captured in model parameters. ## _A. Condition Monitoring_

For the purpose of condition monitoring of the solar farms, we propose to observe the coefficients obtained from regres-

sion. In figure 5 we plot the proportionality constant obtained from one of the _“piece”_ from piece-wise linear model. For normally operating solar panels, this coefficients are expected to remain nearly constant and most of them indeed are slowly varying. A sudden change can be indicative of malfunction in the farm while a gradual change will be representative of aging of solar panels. In figure 5, we can observe both kind of behavior. For the case of mono-crystalline panels, there was some fault in the middle of the year. This information can be used for scheduling the repair/maintenance work to alleviate the cause of under-performance. Similarly, for CIS panels, the coefficient started among the highest values and by the end of second year, it had the least value. Average rate of reduction of this coefficient is about 6.1% per year. This gradual decline in the coefficient value is representative of aging of the panels. Using moving window approach, we can track the performance of the panels and hence can decide to replace the aged panels.

## _B. Robust Power Forecasting_

We observe in previous section that mono-crystalline panel under-performs in the middle of second year. For grid feeding systems, this will results in huge losses not only because of low power output, but also from the penalty associated with it. As mentioned earlier repair/maintenance work is required to address this, however accurate forecast of how much power can be supplied to the grid can at least avoid the losses incurred due to penalty. Thus there is a need for a model which can provide power forecast with reasonable accuracy even when panels are under-performing. In this subsection we propose to use the moving window approach to provide an accurate forecast which is robust to under-performance.

In figure 4, we plot the N-RMSE for all the panel types for both the approach: _Piece-wise linear_ and _Moving window piece-wise linear_ . As we can observe the proposed approach yields either smaller or similar error as compared to the simple piece-wise linear approach. ## V. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK

Declining costs and aggressive targets set by governments around the world have led to increased share of solar PV in the energy market. Solar PV ultra-low maintenance, is a lucrative energy sources however solar farms may under-perform due several reasons, including soiling and dust accumulation, aging, malfunction of equipments, etc. This compels farm owners and operators to do an active condition monitoring of their solar panels. Further, feed-in tariffs require the solar farms to pre-declare the amount of green energy being supplied and failing the unit commitment results in penalties. This drives the need for accurate and robust power forecasting techniques for unit commitment applications.

In this paper, we propose a moving window based approach to address the dual problem of condition monitoring and robust power forecasting. We implemented our methodology on a data set collected from solar farm located in Brunei. We have demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed methodology for both the applications. We are able to detect under performance due sudden malfunction in the panels as well as the gradual aging of the solar panels. Further, we have also demonstrated that moving window approach is superior in power forecasting since it has the capability of capture the variations that may occur during operation. Our approach showed consistently low errors even in the can of malfunction of one of the panels.

In future, we plant to test this moving window approach on more sophisticated and advanced machine learning techniques

such as non-linear regression, support vector machines, random forests, etc. Further, this approach can be deployed in fields to observe the performance of the methodology in a real life scenario. Finally, our approach is generic enough and, can very well be extended to other sources such as wind power, where there are similar types of issues.
